regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unimpeachable until you set it beside core sector growth at 4.8% YoY — down from 5.0% — which covers eight industries accounting for 40% of IIP. The reconciliation is services: PMI Services at 55.2 and credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising two in a row) are doing the heavy lifting that goods production is not. The inversion worth watching: if services credit is the engine, and deposit growth at 17.8% YoY is the fuel tank, the engine is running faster than the tank can refill.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY is being driven by two components that the RBI cannot directly control — fuel at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) and food at 7.74% YoY — while core CPI sits at 3.9% YoY, a 28th-percentile reading that signals domestic demand is not the problem. The gap between headline and core is 164 bps and widening; this is a supply-side shock, not a demand overheat. The second-order trap: the RBI's own inflation forecast has risen to 5.1% YoY, which mathematically rules out a rate cut even as the real economy would welcome one — the RBI is being held hostage by Brent at $113/bbl.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth at 17.8% YoY sounds like a 160 bps gap — manageable. But the CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile) has been falling from 83% precisely because deposit growth accelerated sharply from 9.9% YoY prior, not because credit slowed. NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY (rising two in a row) and corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month signal that the system is routing around bank balance sheets. The historical precedent that matters: the last time the CD ratio sustained above 80% during a credit acceleration cycle, macro-prudential tightening via risk weights followed within two quarters.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is a 38th-percentile rate against a 52nd-percentile CPI — the real rate is barely positive at 29 bps if you use the RBI's own 5.1% YoY inflation forecast as the deflator. That is not a restrictive stance; it is a neutral one that is doing nothing to cool fuel-driven inflation and everything to discourage deposit mobilisation. The signal for housing: average home loan rates at 7.8% p.a. with an affordability index at a 100th-percentile 10.34× price-to-income means the rate pause is not relieving housing stress — it is merely not adding to it.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (up from 16.1%, rising two in a row) alongside capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%) is the strongest simultaneous reading in this cycle. The inversion: capacity utilisation above 75% is historically the threshold at which private capex decisions get made — we are through it, and the data confirms it with credit to industry at 18.2% YoY. The caveat is core sector at 4.8% YoY, down from 5.0%, which means the capex signal is strongest in services and manufacturing equipment, not in the infrastructure backbone of cement, steel, and electricity.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month is a 73rd-percentile reading, but the composition matters more than the headline: passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY are falling two in a row from 26.1%, while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounded sharply. This is the classic India dual-economy split — mass-market rural consumption (two-wheelers) recovering while urban discretionary (passenger vehicles) decelerates. E-commerce GMV at 12.4% YoY (15th percentile) corroborates the urban softness. The GST number is not a demand record; it is partly formalisation reclassifying existing spend, and the vehicle data is the honest proxy.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence that has widened for 2 consecutive months (83.04% → 81.4% → 81% CD ratio). Deposit growth accelerated sharply from 9.9% YoY prior, but credit is outpacing it. NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY (rising 2 in a row) signals non-bank lenders are also competing for wholesale funding. Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month suggests corporates are bypassing banks entirely.","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% — they'll poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; funding costs will spike if CD ratio stays above 80%. Watch for RBI to signal deposit-friendly measures (higher CRR exemptions, VRRR tweaks) within 6 weeks. Tactical short on mid-cap NBFC bonds.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 81% is mid-range historically (73rd percentile), but the acceleration of credit relative to deposits is the stress signal. This ratio preceded tighter liquidity and NBFC funding crises in 2018–19.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Beyond Goods","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest, up from 16.1% prior) with capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%) — both rising 2 in a row. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5%) signals uneven momentum, but credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising 2 in a row) and credit to agriculture at 17.2% YoY (rising 2 in a row) show capex is broadening beyond manufacturing. Office absorption at 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter (up from 4.12 mn sq ft / quarter) signals GCC and IT services are driving real capex, not just credit.","implication":"Overweight capital goods OEMs (Cummins, Escorts, Bharat Electronics) and industrial services (Larsen & Toubro, Thermax). Increase allocation to agri-tech and rural capex plays (IIFC, Mahindra & Mahindra). Avoid pure-play IT services — office absorption is GCC-driven, not traditional IT services expansion. Capex cycle typically runs 18–24 months; lock in positions now.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is at the 74th percentile — historically, this level has preceded 12–18 months of sustained capex and earnings growth. Last time we saw this (2021–22), capex stocks outperformed by 300+ bps.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Momentum Masks Affluent Rotation","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (rising 3 in a row: ₹29,845 → ₹31,961 → ₹32,297 → ₹32,490), but SIP YoY growth at 10.7% (down from 15% → 19.85% → 14%) signals deceleration. SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (down from 10.45 mn prior quarter) — account count is falling while inflows rise. SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (up from ₹16.64 lakh cr) growing faster than account count. Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (up from ₹29,329 cr / month, rising 2 in a row) while NFO collections collapsed to ₹998 cr / month (down from ₹3,051 cr / month, 2nd percentile).","implication":"Average SIP ticket size is rising — affluent investors are entering via SIPs, not mass retail. This is late-cycle behaviour. Rotate from small-cap / mid-cap MF flows (which rely on account growth) to large-cap and dividend-focused funds. Reduce exposure to MF-dependent micro-cap stocks. NFO collapse signals retail is fatigued on new schemes — focus on existing fund performance, not asset gathering.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile historically; however, the divergence between inflows and account growth is a red flag. In 2021–22, similar patterns preceded a 6-month correction in retail-heavy segments.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens Margin Compression","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (up from 20.05% prior, rising 2 in a row) — at the 95th percentile, the highest in the dataset. Brent crude at $113.23 / bbl (flat, but up from $109.7 / bbl 5 periods ago). WTI at $99.33 / bbl (flat). Natural gas at $2.78 / MMBtu (falling 5 in a row from $3.12 / MMBtu) — only gas is easing. FAO food index at 136 (up from 128.5 five periods ago, 61st percentile) adds to input cost pressure. India's headline CPI at 5.54% YoY (up from 4.83%, rising 2 in a row) is being driven by fuel and food.","implication":"Hedge long equity exposure with energy puts or reduce cyclical exposure (auto, cement, fertiliser). Overweight energy stocks (ONGC, Reliance) — they benefit from high crude. Avoid consumer staples with high fuel-dependent logistics (FMCG, QSR). Airlines (IndiGo, SpiceJet) face margin compression; reduce exposure. RBI will struggle to cut rates while fuel inflation stays elevated — expect repo rate to stay at 5.25% p.a. for at least 2 more quarters.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is extreme. Historically, such spikes have preceded 2–3 quarter periods of margin compression in non-energy sectors and RBI rate pause extensions.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Unwinds Carry Trades","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (up from 1% p.a., rising 2 in a row) — at the 100th percentile, the highest in the dataset. Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63%, rising 2 in a row, 68th percentile). ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (up from 2.25%, rising 2 in a row, 63rd percentile). US 10Y Treasury yield at 5.13% (up from 5.12%, 93rd percentile). US PMI composite at 58.4 (up from 56, 91st percentile) signals US growth is strong, but global PMI composite at 54.3 (up from 53.5, 84th percentile) shows divergence. China PMI at 52.1 (up from 50.8, 77th percentile) is recovering but fragile.","implication":"BOJ tightening is unwinding the yen carry trade — expect INR volatility to spike. Reduce leverage in emerging market positions; deleveraging will hit India first. Overweight USD-denominated assets and reduce INR-denominated debt exposure. FII flows to India will remain negative (FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month, 17th percentile) until US rates stabilize. Tactical hedge: long USD/INR calls, short INR-denominated corporate bonds.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile is unprecedented in this dataset. Historically, BOJ tightening cycles have preceded 3–6 month periods of EM currency weakness and carry trade unwinds, with India typically hit hardest due to high carry trade positioning.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakens as FII Flows Turn Negative","data_text":"INR at 95.24 ₹ / USD (up from 94.81 ₹ / USD, rising 2 in a row, 89th percentile) — weakening trend. FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (latest, 17th percentile) — significant outflow. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (latest, 95th percentile) — domestic flows are offsetting FII outflows, but barely. India VIX at 15.762 (up from 15.68, rising 3 in a row, 11th percentile) — volatility is low, masking underlying stress. DXY at 101.56 (flat, 54th percentile) — US dollar strength is moderate, but BOJ tightening is driving yen strength, which pressures INR.","implication":"RBI will need to intervene to defend INR — expect FX reserves to decline modestly over next 2 quarters. Reduce INR-denominated debt exposure; lock in USD borrowing costs now. Overweight exporters (IT, pharma, textiles) — they benefit from INR weakness. Avoid import-heavy sectors (auto, capital goods). If INR breaches 96.50 ₹ / USD, expect RBI to signal tighter liquidity (CRR hike, OMO sales) — this will hurt credit growth and equity valuations.","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile weakness is significant. Historically, such levels have preceded 2–3 quarter periods of RBI intervention and tighter liquidity conditions, with equity markets typically correcting 5–8% in the near term.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Signals GCC Capex, Not IT Services","data_text":"Office absorption at 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter (latest, up from 4.12 mn sq ft / quarter) with office vacancy at 13% (down from 14.5%, 33rd percentile). Nifty IT index is flat (recent: 22,722 → 22,623 → 22,997 → 23,146 → 22,889 → 22,811), but office absorption is accelerating. Rent in Bengaluru at ₹102 / sqft / month (down from ₹109 / sqft / month, 58th percentile) and Mumbai at ₹156 / sqft / month (up from ₹144 / sqft / month, 59th percentile) — rents are diverging by city. Credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising 2 in a row, 79th percentile) is the highest credit growth segment. Contrast: airline passenger traffic at 86.4 mn / month (up from 85.17 mn / month, 35th percentile) — business travel is not accelerating.","implication":"Office absorption is being driven by Global Capability Centers (GCCs) and captive IT operations, NOT traditional IT services firms. This means capex is shifting from IT services (Infosys, TCS, Wipro) to multinational corporates setting up India operations. Reduce overweight on IT services; rotate into commercial real estate (Embassy, Mindspace) and IT infrastructure plays (data centres, co-working). The divergence between office absorption and IT stock performance suggests IT services are losing market share to GCCs — this is a structural headwind for the sector. Falsifiable: if Nifty IT outperforms by > 500 bps over next 2 quarters, GCC thesis is wrong.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption data is sparse (0th percentile historical context), but the cross-domain signal is clear: GCC capex is decoupling from traditional IT services. This pattern preceded a 15–20% underperformance of IT services vs. the broader market in 2022–23.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP Headline — Services Engine, Goods Drag

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY with PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) signals broad expansion — manufacturing PMI at 55.1 and services PMI at 55.2 both above 55.
  • But core sector growth at 4.8% YoY — down from 5.0% — covers 40% of IIP and is decelerating, exposing the goods economy as the weak underbelly.
  • Credit to services at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile, rising two in a row) is the fastest-growing credit segment — services are borrowing to grow while goods production stalls.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounded sharply; passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY fell two in a row from 26.1% — rural mass-market recovering, urban discretionary fading.

The tension: GDP at 7.8% YoY is real but narrow: services credit and rural consumption are carrying a load that goods production and urban discretionary are not sharing. The headline flatters the breadth.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY — a third consecutive month below 5.0% would confirm the goods economy is structurally lagging the services headline.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Re-Acceleration Meets Japanese Repricing — EM Caught Between

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile, rising two in a row) signals the strongest US growth momentum in this cycle — US GDP SAAR at 2.2% SAAR is recovering from 0.7%.
  • But Nikkei 225 fell to 62,908 from a 100th-percentile prior — BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising two in a row) is repricing Japanese equities and unwinding yen carry trades.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.13% yield (93rd percentile) keeps the dollar bid; DXY at 101.56 (54th percentile) is moderate, but BOJ tightening is the underappreciated pressure valve.
  • China PMI Composite at 52.1 (77th percentile) is recovering but China GDP at 4.4% YoY (46th percentile) remains below its own trend — no commodity reflation anchor from Beijing.

The tension: US growth is genuinely re-accelerating, but the BOJ's rate path is the circuit-breaker: every 25 bps of BOJ tightening strengthens the yen, unwinds carry trades, and pulls liquidity from EM — including India.

Bottom line: BOJ's next rate decision is the single most important global event for India's FII flow trajectory — a move to 1.5% p.a. would accelerate the ₹49,935 cr / month outflow already underway.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Holds — But Account Attrition Signals Affluent Rotation

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile, rising three in a row) — the flow is unbroken, but SIP YoY growth at 10.7% YoY has decelerated from 19.85% four months ago.
  • SIP accounts at 10.06 mn — down from 10.45 mn prior quarter — while SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr rose; fewer accounts, larger average ticket size signals affluent consolidation, not mass participation.
  • Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (80th percentile, up from ₹29,329 cr / month) — but NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) show fund houses have stopped launching new products.
  • But FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) — DII at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is absorbing the outflow by the thinnest of margins.

The tension: Domestic flows are holding the market up, but the SIP account decline and NFO collapse suggest the retail base is narrowing to wealthier participants — a structurally thinner support than the headline inflow number implies.

Bottom line: If SIP inflow growth falls below 8% YoY — the level at which account attrition historically outpaces ticket-size expansion — DII absorption of FII outflows becomes arithmetically fragile.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Affordability at 10-Year Worst — NRI Demand Fills the Premium Gap

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (up 8 pp vs prior period), with NRI share within premium/luxury at 25%; remittances at $144.8 bn (16.2% YoY) are the funding source.
  • Affordability index at 10.34× price ÷ income (100th percentile) — the worst on record — explains why domestic mass-market buyers are retreating while NRI dollar-earners absorb premium supply.
  • Hyderabad leads with sales 15% YoY and launches 120% YoY — a supply surge into strong demand; Bengaluru at sales 12% YoY with only 15 months unsold inventory is the tightest market.
  • Office absorption at 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter with GCCs at 42% of occupier mix — but Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit and Mindspace at ₹345/unit are both down sharply from prior, suggesting the REIT market is pricing rate risk, not absorption strength.
  • But Nifty 50 at 22,688 (73rd percentile) and Bank Nifty at 54,926 (90th percentile) remain elevated relative to the earnings risk embedded in fuel-driven margin compression.

The tension: Office absorption and NRI residential demand are structurally sound, but REIT unit prices and equity indices are diverging from fundamentals in opposite directions — REITs underpriced on absorption, equities overpriced on margin risk.

Bottom line: Overweight Bengaluru and Hyderabad residential (NRI-driven premium, tight inventory); hedge Nifty via Bank Nifty puts if fuel inflation sustains above 20% YoY into Q3 earnings.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Match — BOJ, Brent, and the Deposit Gap

The facts:

  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — every 25 bps increment strengthens yen, unwinds carry, and accelerates FII equity outflows already at -₹49,935 cr / month; probability: high, impact: severe.
  • Brent at $113/bbl (79th percentile) — sustained above $110/bbl adds ~$18 bn to India's annual import bill, widens CAD by ~50 bps, and keeps CPI above RBI's 5.1% YoY forecast; probability: high, impact: high.
  • CD ratio at 81% with credit at 19.4% YoY — if deposit growth reverts toward its prior 9.9% YoY trend, the funding gap forces either credit rationing or a deposit rate war that compresses NIMs; probability: medium, impact: high.
  • But affordability index at 10.34× (100th percentile) with home loan rates at 7.8% p.a. — any repo rate hike forced by inflation would push affordability further into record territory and stall the residential cycle.

The tension: All three risks are linked: BOJ tightening pressures INR, INR weakness amplifies Brent's CAD impact, and CAD stress forces RBI toward tightening — which then hits the deposit gap and housing affordability simultaneously.

Bottom line: Watch Brent crude this week — a close above $115/bbl would force RBI to abandon its neutral stance and reprice the entire rate curve, triggering the cascade.

"}
